title: Is UAE tap water safe to drink without a filter?
h1: Is UAE Tap Water Safe to Drink Without a Filter?
primaryQuestion: Is tap water in the UAE safe to drink straight from the tap?
metaTitle: Is UAE Tap Water Safe to Drink?
metaDescription: UAE mains water is desalinated and treated at the plant. What changes it before your tap is distribution and building storage — and what that means for you.
directAnswer: Mains water in the UAE is produced mainly by seawater desalination and leaves the plant treated to a drinking-water standard. The question a filter answers is not about the plant — it is about the journey afterwards. Water travels through distribution pipework and, in most UAE buildings, sits in a ground or rooftop storage tank before reaching your tap. That stage can add sediment, rust from older pipework, a chlorine taste, and — where a tank is poorly maintained — a microbiological risk. Whether you need treatment, and which kind, depends on what your own tap measures, not on a national statement.
keyFacts: UAE mains supply is predominantly desalinated and treated to a drinking-water standard at the plant
Most UAE properties store water on site before use, in a building tank, a villa tank, or a tanker-filled tank
Storage and distribution are where sediment, rust, taste and microbiological risk are introduced
TDS and hardness vary between buildings and even between risers, so a measured reading is the only basis for a decision

sections.heading: What the utility delivers
paragraphs: The emirate utilities — DEWA in Dubai, ADDC in Abu Dhabi, SEWA in Sharjah, and Etihad Water and Electricity across the northern Emirates — supply water produced predominantly by desalination. Desalinated water leaving a plant is low in dissolved solids by design, and it is treated and disinfected before it enters the network.

So the honest starting point is that the water is not being delivered to you dirty. Anyone selling a filter on the premise that UAE mains water is unsafe at source is overstating the case. The reason point-of-use treatment is nonetheless common here is structural, and it has nothing to do with the plant.

sections.heading: What changes between the plant and your glass
paragraphs: Water is blended and distributed across long networks, then — in the overwhelming majority of UAE buildings — held in storage before it is used. An apartment tower fills a tank and lifts water with booster pumps. A villa fills a ground or roof tank. In parts of the northern Emirates and the outlying areas, a tanker fills that tank.
Every one of those stages is an opportunity for something to change:

list.title: Sediment
list.body: Sand and fine particles settle in tanks and are stirred up by refilling and by demand. This is the single most common visible water complaint in the UAE, and it originates in storage rather than in supply.

list.title: Rust and scale from pipework
list.body: Older buildings — parts of Deira, Bur Dubai, older Sharjah blocks — have the oldest risers. Corrosion products flaking off pipework show up as staining and a metallic taste.

list.title: Chlorine taste and odour
list.body: Residual disinfectant is there deliberately, to keep the network safe. It is also the most common taste complaint, and the easiest to treat.

list.title: Microbiological risk in poorly maintained tanks
list.body: A tank that is not cleaned on schedule, particularly at summer temperatures, is the one genuine safety concern in this chain — and it is a concern about the tank, not about the utility.

list.title: Hardness
list.body: Dissolved calcium and magnesium reach your property regardless of storage. This is what scales your kettle, clouds shower glass and shortens appliance life.

sections.heading: Why we will not quote you a TDS figure for your emirate
paragraphs: You will find websites stating a TDS value for Dubai or Abu Dhabi water. Treat them with suspicion. Real values vary with the supply zone, seasonal blending, how long water has been standing in a tank, and when that tank was last cleaned. Two apartments in the same tower can read differently, and the same apartment can read differently before and after a tank clean.

A number that varies that much cannot specify a system. This is why every recommendation should trace back to a reading taken at the tap you actually drink from — and why a ten-minute measurement is worth more than any published figure.

sections.heading: What treatment actually addresses which complaint
paragraphs: Matching the treatment to the complaint is where most money is wasted or saved:

list.title: Chlorine smell, taste, odour
list.body: A carbon stage. Inexpensive, no drain connection needed, no water sent to waste. If this is your only complaint, RO is an expensive way to solve it.

list.title: Visible sediment, rust staining
list.body: A sediment stage — at the point of use for one tap, or at the point of entry to protect the whole property and its appliances.

list.title: Salty, flat or metallic taste; high measured TDS
list.body: Reverse osmosis. It is the only practical household treatment for dissolved content, because sediment and carbon stages pass dissolved salts straight through.

list.title: White scale on taps, glass and inside the kettle
list.body: A softener, at the point of entry. Nothing fitted at the kitchen sink changes scale forming elsewhere in the property.

list.title: Water stored in a tank or delivered by tanker
list.body: Disinfection on the drinking line — UV or a contact-disinfection stage. A sediment or carbon cartridge does not disinfect anything, and this is the most common gap we find in existing installations.

sections.heading: So do you need a filter?
paragraphs: If your water tastes of chlorine, carries visible sediment, leaves scale, or comes from a tank you do not control, then point-of-use treatment is a reasonable investment — and the specific treatment should follow the specific complaint.

If none of those apply and your measured TDS is low, the honest answer is that you may not need to buy anything. That outcome is common enough that it is worth having someone measure before you shop, and worth being sceptical of anyone who recommends a system without measuring.

title: RO vs UV water purifier: which do you need?
h1: RO vs UV Water Purifier: Which Do You Need?
primaryQuestion: Should I choose an RO purifier or a UV purifier?
metaDescription: RO removes dissolved solids; UV inactivates micro-organisms and removes nothing. They solve different problems, and many UAE villas need both.
directAnswer: RO and UV are not competing options — they treat different problems. Reverse osmosis pushes water through a membrane and removes dissolved content, typically rejecting 95 to 99% of total dissolved solids; it is the answer to a salty, flat or metallic taste. UV passes water under an ultraviolet lamp and inactivates bacteria, viruses and cysts without removing anything and without changing the taste; it is the answer to water that has been stored in a tank or delivered by tanker. If your complaint is taste or TDS, you need RO. If your concern is stored water, you need UV. Many UAE villas need both, and in that case the UV stage goes after the filtration, never before it.
keyFacts: RO removes dissolved solids; UV removes nothing at all
UV inactivates upwards of 99.9% of common bacteria and viruses at its rated dose, in clear water
UV requires filtration upstream — particles shield organisms from the light
Neither replaces the other: RO does not disinfect reliably on its own, and UV does not improve taste

sections.heading: What each one actually does
paragraphs: Reverse osmosis forces water at pressure against a semi-permeable membrane. Water passes through; most dissolved salts, metals and larger organic molecules are rejected and carried to the drain. That is a change in what the water is made of.

UV disinfection passes water around a lamp inside a quartz sleeve, at a wavelength that damages micro-organism DNA so they cannot reproduce. Nothing is added and nothing is removed — the organisms are still in the water, inactivated. That is a change in whether what is living in the water can do anything.

sections.heading: The comparison that matters
When RO is the right answer
paragraphs: RO is what you want when the problem is dissolved:

list.title: Salty, flat or metallic taste
list.body: A taste complaint that is not chlorine is usually dissolved content, and carbon will not change it.

list.title: High measured TDS
list.body: Where a reading is genuinely high, no cartridge filter changes it. RO or distillation are the only practical options and distillation is impractical at home.

list.title: Apartments
list.body: You cannot treat the building's supply, so treating the drinking outlet thoroughly is the whole available strategy.

sections.heading: When UV is the right answer
paragraphs: UV is what you want when the problem is stored:

list.title: Villas on tank or tanker supply
list.body: The main UAE case. Storage introduces a risk that filtration does not address.

list.title: Seasonally used properties
list.body: Water standing in a system for months is a different proposition from water standing for a weekend.

list.title: Disinfection without chemicals
list.body: UV adds nothing — no dosing, no by-products, no taste change.

sections.heading: Why they are usually fitted together in UAE villas
paragraphs: A very large share of UAE properties store water before using it. That means the two problems genuinely coexist: dissolved content that RO addresses, and a storage risk that UV addresses. Fitting one and calling the job done leaves a real gap.

The order is not negotiable. Filtration first, UV last on the drinking line. Particles and turbidity shield organisms from the light, so a UV chamber fed unfiltered water is delivering far less protection than its rating implies. Any quotation for UV that does not include sediment filtration upstream is quoting less protection than it appears to.

sections.heading: Two mistakes we are regularly called to correct

list.title: UV fitted as a standalone answer to a safety worry
list.body: Without filtration ahead of it, and often without any monitoring, so a failed lamp goes unnoticed for months. A UV chamber with no power is a plain pipe.

list.title: RO fitted expecting it to handle a tank problem
list.body: RO membranes are a physical barrier and do reduce microbiological load, but a residential RO system is not a validated disinfection stage, and the tubing and tank downstream of the membrane are not sterile. On stored supply, UV is the stage that addresses this.

sections.heading: The lamp question nobody expects
paragraphs: A UV lamp's output falls long before it stops glowing. Disinfection depends on dose — intensity multiplied by exposure time — so a lamp at the end of its rated life can look perfect while delivering too little ultraviolet to be relied on. That is why the interval is annual, based on running hours, and why the quartz sleeve is cleaned or replaced at the same visit: film or scale on the sleeve blocks the light before it reaches the water.

comparison.caption: RO and UV compared on what each is asked to do

rows.label: Inactivates bacteria and viruses
values: Reduces load, but not a validated disinfection stage
Yes — upwards of 99.9% at rated dose in clear water

rows.label: Needs electricity
values: Only if a booster pump is fitted

rows.label: Needs filtration upstream
values: Yes, or the dose is not delivered

verdict: Choose RO for a taste or TDS problem, UV for a stored-water problem, and both where a villa has both — with UV placed after the filtration. If someone offers you one as a substitute for the other, they are answering a different question from the one you asked.

title: RO vs water softener: they solve different problems
h1: RO vs Water Softener: Which One Fixes Your Problem?
primaryQuestion: Do I need an RO purifier or a water softener?
metaDescription: An RO purifier treats one tap for drinking. A softener treats the whole property for limescale. Fitting the wrong one is the expensive mistake.
directAnswer: They are not alternatives. An RO purifier treats one outlet and addresses dissolved content in the water you drink. A softener treats the whole incoming supply and removes the calcium and magnesium that scale your geyser, kettle, washing machine, shower glass and taps. Fitting RO does nothing about limescale anywhere else in the property, and fitting a softener does not make water suitable for drinking on its own. If you have both a taste complaint and white scale on your fittings, you are looking at two devices.
keyFacts: RO is point-of-use and treats dissolved solids; a softener is point-of-entry and treats hardness
Scale on taps, glass and kettle elements is a hardness problem — no kitchen filter changes it
A softener does not purify water for drinking; other dissolved solids pass through
A softener ahead of an RO system extends the membrane's life, which is why villas often have both

sections.heading: The distinction in one sentence each

list.title: RO purifier
list.body: A membrane at one tap that rejects most dissolved content, so the water you drink and cook with has a different composition. It changes nothing about the water reaching your shower or your washing machine.

list.title: Water softener
list.body: An ion-exchange vessel on the incoming supply that swaps calcium and magnesium for sodium, so scale stops forming everywhere in the property. It changes nothing about whether the water is suitable to drink.

sections.heading: How to tell which problem you have
paragraphs: The symptoms point cleanly in one direction or the other, which is why this is an easy diagnosis to get right and an expensive one to get wrong.

list.title: You have a hardness problem if
list.body: There is white, chalky deposit on taps and shower glass, spotting on glassware, a furred kettle element, laundry that feels stiff, or skin that feels tight after a shower. These are all the same cause showing up in different places.

list.title: You have a dissolved-solids problem if
list.body: Your drinking water tastes salty, flat or metallic, and a measured TDS reading is high. Note that this is about taste and measurement, not about anything visible.

list.title: You have both if
list.body: Both lists describe your property — which is common in UAE villas, and is the situation where fitting only one of the two leaves the other complaint completely untouched.

sections.heading: The comparison
The mistake that costs the most
paragraphs: The expensive version of this mistake is fitting an under-sink RO in response to limescale. The customer sees scale, understands that they have a water problem, buys the most thorough-sounding water treatment available, and then finds the shower glass still clouds and the kettle still furs — because the RO is treating one tap and the scale is forming everywhere else.

The reverse happens too, though it costs less: a softener fitted in response to a taste complaint. Softened water is not low-TDS water; the hardness has been exchanged for sodium, and the dissolved load is broadly similar. A taste complaint that was not about hardness will still be there.

sections.heading: Why the two work well together
paragraphs: Hardness scales RO membranes and filter housings just as it scales a geyser. A softener upstream of a drinking-water system therefore extends the consumable life of the system downstream — which is part of why the standard specification on a UAE villa is point-of-entry treatment plus a point-of-use drinking system, rather than one or the other.

One detail worth getting right at installation: if an irrigation line shares the incoming supply, take it off ahead of the softener. Plants gain nothing from softened water, and the resin's exchange capacity is wasted on landscaping.

comparison.caption: RO purifier and water softener compared

rows.label: Where it is fitted
values: On the incoming supply (point of entry)

rows.label: Consumables
values: Salt, and resin over the long term

rows.label: Typical UAE property
values: Villas and buildings, where you control the incoming line

verdict: Match the device to the symptom: scale means a softener, taste and TDS mean RO. In a UAE villa with both symptoms, fit both — softener at the point of entry, RO at the kitchen sink — and take the irrigation line off ahead of the softener.

title: Tank vs tankless RO: which suits your kitchen?
h1: Tank vs Tankless RO Purifier: Which Suits Your Kitchen?
primaryQuestion: Should I buy a tanked or a tankless RO water purifier?
metaDescription: A tanked RO stores purified water and delivers a fast flow; a tankless one takes far less space. Cupboard depth and household size decide it.
directAnswer: Neither is better — they trade different things. A tanked system stores several litres of purified water, so it delivers a fast flow from a modest pump, but the tank takes cupboard space and water sits in storage between draws. A tankless system purifies as you draw, so nothing is stored and it needs far less depth, but it requires a higher-output membrane and a pump to deliver a usable flow rate, which raises the purchase price. Tight apartment cupboard: tankless. Large family drawing several litres at once: tanked.
keyFacts: Tanked delivers faster flow because the water is already purified and stored
Tankless takes much less cupboard depth because there is no storage vessel
Tankless costs more for the same filtration — you pay for the space saving and on-demand behaviour
A tank's air charge is a maintenance item; losing it presents as low pressure at the faucet

sections.heading: Why the difference exists at all
paragraphs: An RO membrane produces water slowly. That is inherent — it is a pressure-driven separation, not a filter that water simply flows through. A residential membrane cannot fill a jug at the rate a tap can.

There are only two ways around that. Store purified water ahead of demand, which is what a tank does. Or make the membrane and pump big enough to keep up with demand as it happens, which is what a tankless system does. Everything else about the comparison follows from that single engineering choice.

sections.heading: The comparison
How to decide in about two minutes

list.title: Measure the cupboard, including depth behind the waste trap
list.body: This is the decisive measurement and the one people skip. Behind the trap is where the space actually runs out. If a unit plus a separate tank will not fit, the decision is made for you.

list.title: Count how much water you draw at once
list.body: Filling a two-litre jug is easy for either. Filling a pot for cooking plus several bottles, back to back, is where on-demand production starts to feel slow. A larger household is the case for a tank.

list.title: Check your feed pressure
list.body: Both types are hurt by low pressure, but tankless is hurt more, because it has no reservoir to draw on while the membrane catches up. On a high floor, confirm pressure before choosing tankless.

list.title: Decide how you feel about stored water
list.body: Water in a tank stands between draws. It is not unsafe, but taste flattens if the household draws little, and the first glass after a few days is noticeably different. Some people care about this; most do not once it is explained.

sections.heading: The maintenance difference nobody mentions at the point of sale
paragraphs: A tanked system has one extra failure mode: the tank's air charge. A pressure tank holds purified water against a diaphragm with a charge of air behind it. Lose the charge and the tank still fills with water but cannot push it out, which presents at the faucet as low pressure — a symptom that people almost always attribute to the membrane.

It is quick to diagnose and quick to correct, and it is the single most common reason we are called out to a tanked system for 'low pressure'. A tankless system does not have this failure mode, which is a genuine, if unglamorous, advantage.

rows.label: Pump requirement
values: Modest, or none with good pressure

rows.label: Best suited to
values: Tight cupboards, smaller households, countertop use

verdict: Measure the cupboard first and count your peak draw second. If both fit a tanked system, it is the cheaper and better-buffered choice. If the cupboard is tight, tankless exists precisely for that, and the price difference buys space rather than better water.

title: How often should RO filters be replaced?
h1: How Often Should RO Filters Be Replaced in the UAE?
primaryQuestion: What is the replacement schedule for RO filters and membranes?
metaTitle: How Often to Replace RO Filters
metaDescription: Pre-filters every 6 months, membrane every 2–3 years, UV lamp annually — and why UAE storage tanks shorten every one of those intervals.
directAnswer: As a working schedule: sediment and carbon pre-filters every 6 months, the RO membrane every 2 to 3 years, the post-carbon or mineral stage every 12 months, and a UV lamp every 12 months. Those are starting points, not rules. In the UAE, sediment loading from building and villa storage tanks is higher than manufacturer schedules assume, so pre-filters often need attention sooner — and on a tanker-fed property, considerably sooner. The honest interval comes from what the removed cartridges actually look like on your property.
keyFacts: Sediment and carbon: about 6 months, sooner on tank-fed or tanker-fed supply
RO membrane: typically 2 to 3 years, judged on TDS rejection rather than the calendar
Post-carbon or mineral stage: about 12 months — this is the stage behind most taste complaints
UV lamp: 12 months on running hours, whether or not it still lights

sections.heading: Why one interval for the whole system is wrong
paragraphs: The stages age by completely different mechanisms, which is why a single service date for everything is a compromise rather than a schedule.

list.title: Sediment cartridges block
list.body: They fill up with what they have caught. This at least announces itself as reduced flow — the only stage that gives you a warning.

list.title: Carbon exhausts
list.body: Carbon adsorbs until it is saturated, then quietly stops working while passing water perfectly normally. There is no symptom until the chlorine taste returns — by which point chlorine has been reaching your membrane.

list.title: Membranes lose rejection gradually
list.body: A membrane does not fail; it declines. Treated TDS creeps up and production slows. Judging it by date rather than by reading either wastes money or wastes the membrane.

list.title: UV lamps lose output while still glowing
list.body: Output decays steadily against a dose requirement that does not. A lamp at the end of its life looks identical to a new one.

sections.heading: The interval that protects everything else
paragraphs: If you only get one interval right, make it the carbon stage. Standard RO membranes are thin-film composite elements, and chlorine destroys them. The carbon cartridge is what stands between residual disinfectant in your supply and the most expensive part of the system.

This is why we see membranes replaced two and three times more often than they should be. The membrane is not failing early because it was a poor membrane; it is failing early because the cartridge in front of it was left in for a year.

sections.heading: What makes UAE intervals shorter

list.title: Storage tanks
list.body: Most UAE properties hold water before using it. Sediment settles in tanks and is stirred up by refilling. A sediment cartridge that lasts a year on continuous mains supply can be finished in a few months here.

list.title: Tanker delivery
list.body: The most demanding duty. Sand and rust picked up in handling go straight into the pre-filter. On these properties a self-cleaning pre-filter at the point of entry — rinsed through a valve instead of replaced — usually pays for itself quickly.

list.title: Heat
list.body: Higher ambient temperatures accelerate biological growth inside housings and standing water. This is why sanitising the housings at every cartridge change matters more here than in a temperate climate.

list.title: Household size
list.body: A family of six draws through the system several times faster than a couple. The consumables do not care about the calendar; they care about litres.

sections.heading: How to tell your membrane is finished
paragraphs: Measure, do not guess. Two indicators, both easy:

list.title: Rising treated TDS
list.body: If the purified reading climbs towards a fifth of the feed reading, rejection has degraded materially. A unit with an on-board TDS readout gives you this for free; otherwise a technician reads it at each service.

list.title: Slower production
list.body: A tanked system taking noticeably longer to refill, or a tankless one delivering more slowly than it used to. Check the pre-filters and the tank charge first, though — both cause the same symptom and both are far cheaper.

sections.heading: A practical schedule to actually follow
paragraphs: Write the date on the housing, or on a label inside the cupboard door, every time a cartridge is changed. It sounds trivial; it is the difference between a schedule and an intention.

Better still, do not rely on remembering at all. The failure mode is never someone deciding to skip a service — it is six months passing while the water still comes out of the tap and nothing prompts anyone. That is the specific problem a maintenance contract solves, and it is the honest reason to consider one.

title: Hard water and limescale in the UAE
h1: Hard Water and Limescale in the UAE: Causes and Fixes
primaryQuestion: What causes limescale in UAE homes and how do I stop it?
metaTitle: Hard Water & Limescale in the UAE
metaDescription: Limescale is dissolved calcium and magnesium. Why nothing at the kitchen sink fixes it, what a softener does, and what to be sceptical of.
directAnswer: Limescale is dissolved calcium and magnesium coming out of solution — when hard water evaporates or is heated, those minerals stay behind as the white, chalky deposit on shower glass, taps and inside a kettle. It is not dirt and it is not a sign the water is unsafe. Because it forms everywhere the water goes, nothing fitted at the kitchen sink changes it. Reducing hardness at the point of entry, with an ion-exchange softener, is the only treatment that stops it forming rather than cleaning it up afterwards.
keyFacts: Limescale is dissolved hardness minerals, deposited when water evaporates or is heated
It forms at every outlet, so point-of-use filters cannot address it
An ion-exchange softener at the point of entry is the treatment that prevents it forming
Scale on heating elements is both a failure risk and a running-cost increase

sections.heading: Where you are seeing it, and why there
paragraphs: The pattern of where scale appears tells you exactly what is happening, and it is always the same two triggers: evaporation and heat.

list.title: Shower glass and taps
list.body: Water evaporates and leaves the minerals behind. This is the most visible symptom and the one people notice first.

list.title: Inside the kettle
list.body: Heat drives the minerals out of solution onto the element. A furred element is the clearest possible demonstration of what is dissolved in your water.

list.title: Geyser and washing machine
list.body: The same process, on the components you cannot see. This is where hardness costs real money, because a scaled heating element runs less efficiently and eventually fails.

list.title: Glassware and laundry
list.body: Spotting on glasses, stiff towels, and needing more detergent to lather. Hard water and soap do not get on.

list.title: Skin and hair after showering
list.body: The tight, dry feeling many UAE residents assume is the climate. Some of it is the extra soap hard water demands.

sections.heading: Why your kitchen filter has not helped
paragraphs: This is the most common misunderstanding we encounter, and it costs people the most. An under-sink filter — even a very good RO system — treats water at one tap. The water going to your shower, your geyser and your washing machine is untouched, so the scale continues to form exactly as before.

It is worth being blunt about it: if your complaint is limescale and someone recommends an under-sink RO, they have not addressed your problem. RO is excellent at what it does. What it does is not this.

sections.heading: What an ion-exchange softener actually does
paragraphs: A softener is a vessel of resin with a control valve on top. Hard water passing through gives up its calcium and magnesium to the resin and takes on a small amount of sodium in exchange. When the resin's capacity is used up, the valve draws brine from a salt tank through the resin, displacing the accumulated hardness, and flushes the lot to the drain.

Two consequences worth knowing. First: the salt is flushed away, not passed into your supply — softened water does not taste salty, and if yours does, something has genuinely failed and is worth calling about. Second: the sizing depends on both your measured hardness and your actual demand. A softener specified from household size alone is specified from half the information, and it will either regenerate constantly or deliver hard water part of the time.

sections.heading: Getting the installation right

list.title: Protect the resin
list.body: A sediment and carbon stage ahead of the softener costs little and materially extends resin life. On a tank-fed or tanker-fed property, sediment reaching the resin bed is difficult to recover from.

list.title: Take the irrigation off first
list.body: If a landscaping line shares the incoming supply, branch it before the softener. Plants gain nothing from softened water and the exchange capacity is simply wasted.

list.title: Plan the drain and the salt
list.body: Regeneration needs a drain. Salt needs carrying to the tank. Both are much easier to solve at installation than to live with afterwards.

list.title: Set the valve to your reading
list.body: Leaving factory defaults in place is the most common reason a correctly sized softener disappoints. Commissioning includes programming it to your measured hardness and usage.

sections.heading: What to be sceptical of
paragraphs: Hardness is a large enough problem in the UAE that it attracts a lot of confident marketing. Two things to hold at arm's length.

Physical, magnetic and electronic 'descalers' claim to change how scale forms without removing hardness. The evidence for them is much weaker than the advertising suggests, and they do not reduce hardness — a hardness test after installation reads the same as before. If a device cannot show a change in a hardness reading, be careful about what you are being asked to believe.
And be sceptical of any recommendation made without a hardness measurement. It takes minutes, it determines the resin volume, and without it the sizing is guesswork.

title: How to reduce the TDS of your drinking water
h1: How to Reduce TDS in Drinking Water
primaryQuestion: How do I lower the TDS of my drinking water at home?
metaDescription: Reverse osmosis is the only practical household treatment for dissolved solids. What TDS does and does not tell you, and why low TDS tastes flat.
directAnswer: Reverse osmosis is the practical answer at home: a membrane rejects most dissolved content, typically 95 to 99% of total dissolved solids. No cartridge filter can do this, because sediment and carbon stages target particles, chlorine, taste and odour, and dissolved salts pass straight through them. Distillation also works but is impractical at household scale. Worth knowing before you start: very low TDS water tastes flat to most people, which is why a remineralising post-stage is common on UAE installations — and TDS is a blunt instrument that tells you how much is dissolved, not what.
keyFacts: RO typically rejects 95–99% of total dissolved solids; cartridge filters reject essentially none
TDS measures quantity dissolved, not identity — a low reading is not by itself proof of safety
Very low TDS water tastes flat; a mineral or alkaline post-stage addresses that
Boiling does not reduce TDS — it concentrates it as water evaporates

sections.heading: What TDS is, and what it is not
paragraphs: Total dissolved solids is the combined concentration of everything dissolved in the water — mineral salts, metals, some organics. A handheld meter estimates it by measuring electrical conductivity, which is why it is cheap and instant.

That convenience is also its limitation. TDS is a quantity, not an identity. A reading of 300 could be largely harmless calcium and magnesium, or it could include something you would rather not drink; the meter cannot distinguish. Equally, a very low reading does not prove water is safe — it says nothing about bacteria, which have almost no effect on conductivity. If you have a specific contaminant concern, laboratory analysis is the honest route, and anyone telling you a handheld meter answers it is overselling the instrument.

sections.heading: What actually reduces TDS

list.title: Reverse osmosis — yes
list.body: The practical household answer. Water is forced against a semi-permeable membrane that rejects dissolved content and sends it to the drain. Rejection depends on feed pressure, temperature and the membrane's condition.

list.title: Distillation — yes, but impractically
list.body: Boiling and condensing removes dissolved solids effectively. At household scale it is slow, energy-hungry and produces small volumes. It is a laboratory method, not a kitchen one.

list.title: Deionisation — yes, but not for drinking
list.body: Ion-exchange resins can strip dissolved ions to very low levels, which is why the technique is used industrially. It is not a domestic drinking-water solution.

sections.heading: What does not reduce TDS, despite common belief

list.title: Sediment and carbon filters
list.body: They improve what you can see, smell and taste. Dissolved salts pass through unchanged. A TDS reading before and after a carbon filter is essentially identical.

list.title: Boiling
list.body: Boiling kills organisms — genuinely useful — but as water evaporates the dissolved solids stay behind, so the concentration in what remains actually rises.

list.title: A water softener
list.body: A softener exchanges calcium and magnesium for sodium. The hardness falls; the total dissolved load does not meaningfully change. Softened water is not low-TDS water.

list.title: Magnetic and electronic descalers
list.body: These claim to alter how scale forms. They do not reduce dissolved content, and a TDS or hardness reading after installation reads the same as before.

sections.heading: The taste problem nobody warns you about
paragraphs: Water stripped to very low TDS tastes flat. Not bad — flat. Most people find that unpleasant enough to notice within a day, and it is the leading reason people report being unhappy with a brand-new RO system that is working perfectly.

The fix is a remineralising or alkaline post-stage, which adds a small, controlled mineral content back. It is worth deciding about deliberately rather than being defaulted into it — and worth knowing that if your RO water tastes flat and there is no mineral stage fitted, the system is not faulty.

sections.heading: Getting the most out of an RO system

list.title: Feed it enough pressure
list.body: Rejection falls and production slows on inadequate pressure. On a high floor or in an older building, a booster pump is part of the system rather than an accessory.

list.title: Keep the carbon stage current
list.body: Chlorine destroys standard membranes. The carbon cartridge is what protects the part that does the actual TDS reduction.

list.title: Judge the membrane by reading, not by date
list.body: Rising treated TDS is the signal. A membrane replaced on a calendar is either replaced too early or left too long.

list.title: Measure your own feed first
list.body: If your feed TDS is already low, RO is an expensive way to solve a problem you may not have. Ten minutes with a meter answers this before you spend anything.

author: aquapure-technical-team

title: Why is my RO water purifier leaking?
h1: Why Is My RO Water Purifier Leaking?
primaryQuestion: My RO purifier is leaking — what is causing it and what should I do?
metaTitle: Why Is My RO Purifier Leaking?
metaDescription: RO leaks are almost always at a joint. How to stop the damage in thirty seconds, then find the source: O-rings, push-fit tubes, tank fittings.
directAnswer: Almost always at a joint rather than through a component. The usual causes are a push-fit tube that was not seated fully or has been disturbed, a perished O-ring in a filter housing after a cartridge change, a housing overtightened until it deformed, a cracked storage-tank fitting, or a faucet base that has loosened. Do this first: close the feed valve at the mains connection, then the tank valve, then dry everything so you can see where water reappears. Do not keep running the system while you diagnose — an under-sink leak damages the cabinet long before it reaches your floor.
keyFacts: Close the feed valve first — it stops the damage immediately
Most leaks are at joints, not through components
A leak found at the highest wet point is usually the source; water travels down
A perished O-ring after a cartridge change is the single most common cause

sections.heading: Do this before anything else
paragraphs: Thirty seconds of the right actions saves the cabinet.

list.title: Close the feed valve
list.body: It is the small valve where the system tees off your cold supply, usually at the back of the cupboard. Turning it off stops water entering the system at all.

list.title: Close the tank valve
list.body: On a tanked system, the valve on top of the storage tank. This stops stored water continuing to feed the leak.

list.title: Dry everything and put paper down
list.body: You cannot find a leak in a wet cupboard. Dry it, lay kitchen paper under the unit, and you will see exactly where water reappears and in what order.

list.title: Do not run it to 'check'
list.body: The instinct to turn it back on and watch is understandable and expensive. Diagnose dry.

sections.heading: The usual suspects, in order of how often we find them

list.title: A perished housing O-ring
list.body: The most common cause, and it usually appears shortly after a cartridge change. The O-ring is compressed, ages in heat, and does not re-seat reliably once disturbed. New O-rings should be standard at every cartridge change, not an optional extra.

list.title: An overtightened housing
list.body: If a housing needed force to stop weeping, the O-ring was already the problem — and the force may have deformed the bowl or damaged the thread. Once deformed, no amount of tightening seals it.

list.title: A push-fit tube not fully seated
list.body: These fittings grip and seal in one motion, and a tube pushed in only most of the way will hold for weeks before letting go. Also common after someone has moved things around under the sink.

list.title: A tube cut at an angle
list.body: An angled cut cannot seal squarely against the fitting's O-ring. This is why a leaking push-fit joint is cut back and re-cut square rather than simply pushed in harder.

list.title: A cracked storage-tank fitting
list.body: The plastic port on the tank is a stress point, particularly if the tank has been knocked or the tube has been pulled. Usually shows as a slow weep at the top of the tank.

list.title: A loose faucet base
list.body: The drinking faucet seals against the sink or worktop from below. It loosens over time with use and shows up as water appearing around the tap, or inside the cupboard directly beneath it.

list.title: A weeping drain saddle
list.body: The connection to the sink waste. The least obvious leak, because it drips into a cabinet floor that people rarely look at, and the one most often found by smell rather than sight.

sections.heading: How to trace it properly
paragraphs: Water travels down and sideways, so the wet patch is rarely the source. Work from the top of the system downwards, and look for the highest wet point rather than the largest one.

With the cupboard dry, open the feed valve alone and wait. If water appears before the tank valve is opened, the leak is on the pressurised feed side — the housings, the pre-filters, the membrane housing. If it only appears once the tank valve is open, look at the tank fitting, the post-filter and the faucet line.

sections.heading: What you can reasonably do yourself, and what you should not

list.title: Reasonable
list.body: Closing the valves. Drying and observing. Hand-tightening a faucet base nut. Reseating a push-fit tube after cutting it back square with a proper tube cutter.

list.title: Not reasonable
list.body: Forcing a housing tighter. Reusing an O-ring that has already failed. Sealing a joint with tape or compound — push-fit and O-ring joints are engineered to seal without either, and adding them usually makes the leak worse. And leaving a system running with a known leak because it is 'only a drip'.

sections.heading: Why this happens more in the UAE
paragraphs: Heat. Plastic housings, O-rings and push-fit tubing all age faster at higher ambient temperatures, and an under-sink cabinet next to an oven, or a plant room with no shade, runs hotter than the numbers on the datasheet assume. Components that would give five years in a temperate climate can perish sooner here.

That is a maintenance implication rather than a reason for alarm: O-rings and tubing are cheap, they are accessible at every service visit, and replacing them proactively is far cheaper than replacing a kitchen cabinet.

author: aquapure-technical-team

title: Why does my RO purifier have low water pressure?
h1: Why Does My RO Purifier Have Low Water Pressure?
primaryQuestion: My RO purifier flow has dropped — what is wrong?
metaDescription: Low flow from an RO faucet is usually a blocked pre-filter or a flat storage tank charge — not the membrane. Work through the causes cheapest first.
directAnswer: In order of how often we find it: a blocked sediment or carbon pre-filter, which starves the membrane; a storage tank that has lost its air charge, so it holds water but cannot push it out; low incoming mains pressure, common on higher floors and fixable with a booster pump; a fouled membrane near the end of its life; or a kinked or partially closed feed line, often after someone has moved things under the sink. The first two account for most cases and both are quick to check — which is why replacing the membrane first is the most expensive way to guess.
keyFacts: Blocked pre-filters and a flat tank charge cause most low-flow complaints
A tank that has lost its air charge fills with water but cannot deliver it
Low feed pressure needs a booster pump, not a larger membrane
The membrane is the last thing to suspect and the most expensive to replace speculatively

sections.heading: Work through it cheapest first
paragraphs: This order is not about saving effort. These genuinely are the most common causes, and testing them is fast.

list.title: 1. Blocked pre-filters
list.body: A sediment or carbon cartridge that has filled up restricts flow to the membrane, and a starved membrane produces slowly. If your cartridges are past due — or you cannot remember when they were changed — this is your answer more often than not.

list.title: 2. Storage tank air charge
list.body: A pressure tank holds purified water against a diaphragm with air behind it. Lose that charge and the tank fills but cannot push out. The tell is a tank that feels heavy and full while the faucet delivers a trickle that stops almost immediately.

list.title: 3. Low incoming pressure
list.body: Very common on high floors and in older buildings. Measure static pressure at the cold tap. If it is low, the system was always going to underperform and the fix is a booster pump.

list.title: 4. Fouled or exhausted membrane
list.body: Genuinely does cause slow production — but usually alongside a rising treated TDS reading. Membrane alone, with normal pre-filters, a good tank charge and adequate feed pressure, is the least common of the five.

list.title: 5. A restricted or closed feed line
list.body: A kinked tube, or a feed valve knocked partially closed. Worth ten seconds of looking, because it happens more often than anyone admits — usually after a plumber, a pest-control visit, or a reorganisation of the cupboard.

sections.heading: How to tell a tank problem from a membrane problem
paragraphs: The pattern of the flow distinguishes them, and it is a genuinely useful diagnostic you can do yourself.

A flat tank charge gives you a short burst of reasonable flow that dies away almost immediately, because you are only getting the water that gravity and residual pressure will give up. A failing membrane gives you a steady but slow flow that keeps going, because production is the limit rather than delivery.
If the faucet delivers a weak stream indefinitely, look at production — pre-filters, pressure, membrane. If it delivers briefly and stops, look at the tank.

sections.heading: Why a booster pump is a specification, not an upsell
paragraphs: An RO membrane is a pressure-driven device. Below its design pressure, three things happen at once: production slows, the proportion of water sent to the drain rises, and rejection falls slightly — so you get less water, waste more, and it is marginally less well purified.

This is why we measure static pressure before quoting, and why on an upper floor a pump belongs in the original specification. A system sold without the pump it needed will be reported as faulty within months, and the customer will be told the membrane needs replacing. It does not.

sections.heading: Tankless systems and low pressure
paragraphs: A tankless system feels low feed pressure immediately, because it has no reservoir to draw on while the membrane catches up. There is no tank charge to check either, which removes one cause from the list but makes the remaining ones more noticeable.
On a tankless unit, a sudden drop in flow points hard at the pre-filters or the pump. Many have a low-pressure warning light, which is worth trusting.

sections.heading: When to stop investigating and call

list.title: You have changed the pre-filters and it is no better
list.body: Time for readings — feed pressure, tank pressure, feed and treated TDS. Guessing past this point gets expensive.

list.title: Flow dropped suddenly rather than gradually
list.body: Gradual decline is consumables. A sudden change is usually a valve, a pump or a kink, and it is worth finding rather than living with.

list.title: Flow is low and the drain runs more than it used to
list.body: That combination points at the membrane or the flow restrictor and is worth diagnosing properly.

title: Choosing a water purifier for a Dubai apartment
h1: Choosing a Water Purifier for a Dubai Apartment
primaryQuestion: What is the best water purifier for a Dubai apartment?
metaTitle: Water Purifier for a Dubai Apartment
metaDescription: In an apartment you treat one tap, not the building. The three measurements that decide the system: cupboard depth, floor pressure, household size.
directAnswer: In an apartment the choice is narrower than the market suggests, because you are treating one outlet rather than the building: an under-sink RO system in almost every case. Three constraints decide which one. Cupboard depth behind the waste trap decides tanked versus tankless. Static pressure at your floor decides whether a booster pump is part of the system. Household size decides whether stored capacity matters. Measure all three before you shop, and measure your water — if your TDS is low and the only complaint is a chlorine taste, a carbon filter fixes it for a fraction of the cost.
keyFacts: An under-sink system needs no building approval and no work on the riser
Cupboard depth behind the waste trap is the measurement that decides tanked vs tankless
Weak pressure on upper floors starves an RO membrane — a pump is a specification, not an accessory
If your only complaint is chlorine taste and your TDS is low, carbon is the cheaper correct answer

sections.heading: Why an apartment narrows the choice
paragraphs: Everything upstream of your front door belongs to the building. The incoming supply, the storage tanks, the booster pumps and the risers are not yours to treat, and work on any of them needs written approval from building management — which for a single household is rarely worth pursuing.

So the whole available strategy is to treat the outlet you drink from, thoroughly. That is not a compromise: point-of-use treatment is exactly the right tool for improving drinking water, and it is the same technology a villa uses at its kitchen sink.

sections.heading: The three measurements to take before you shop

list.title: Cupboard depth, behind the waste trap
list.body: Not the width, and not the depth at the front. The usable space is what remains behind the trap and the pipework, and it is routinely much less than people expect in newer Dubai towers. If a unit plus a separate storage tank will not fit, you need a tankless system and the decision is made.

list.title: Static pressure at your cold tap
list.body: An RO membrane is pressure-driven. Below its design pressure it produces slowly, sends more water to the drain and rejects marginally less. On upper floors and in older buildings this is common enough that a booster pump belongs in the original quotation.

list.title: Your household's peak draw
list.body: Filling a jug is easy for any system. Filling a pot plus several bottles back to back is where on-demand production feels slow. A larger household is the case for stored capacity.

sections.heading: And measure the water, before you assume RO
paragraphs: This is where money is most often wasted. RO is the right answer for a dissolved-solids problem — water that tastes salty, flat or metallic, with a high measured TDS. It is an expensive answer for a chlorine problem, which a carbon stage fixes at a fraction of the cost, with no drain connection and no water sent to waste.

Two apartments in the same Dubai tower can read differently, which is why no published figure for the emirate can specify your system. Ten minutes with a meter at your own tap decides which of the two situations you are in.

sections.heading: Tanked or tankless, decided by your cupboard

list.title: Tanked, if it fits
list.body: Cheaper for equivalent filtration, faster flow at the faucet because the water is already purified, and buffered against pressure dips. The costs are cupboard space and one extra maintenance item — the tank's air charge.

list.title: Tankless, if space is the constraint
list.body: Slim upright casing, nothing stored, far less depth. You pay more for the same filtration, and the flow is limited by production rate rather than by a reservoir. Also the better choice if you dislike the idea of water standing between draws.

sections.heading: Practical details specific to apartment living

list.title: The faucet hole
list.body: A dedicated drinking faucet needs a hole. Ask whether an existing tap hole or sink knockout can be used before anyone drills a stone worktop — this matters twice over in a rented apartment, and it is usually possible.

list.title: Tenancy and reversibility
list.body: An under-sink system connects to existing plumbing and can be removed cleanly, which is what makes it viable in rented property. Keep the original tap blank if one is removed.

list.title: Moving out
list.body: A good system is worth taking. Relocation is a single job — drained, sanitised, transported and recommissioned at the new address, with the new property's pressure checked rather than assumed.

list.title: Cartridge availability
list.body: Prefer standard formats. A system built around proprietary consumables waits for a delivery every time it needs a service.

sections.heading: What an apartment cannot fix, and it is worth knowing
paragraphs: If your complaint is a chlorine smell in the shower, sediment in the washing machine, or limescale on the bathroom glass, no under-sink system will change it. Those are point-of-entry problems, and in an apartment the point of entry is the building's.

That is an honest limitation rather than a reason to buy something bigger. Limescale in particular is worth understanding before spending: an under-sink RO fitted in response to shower-glass scale is the most common expensive mistake we are called to explain.

title: Whole house water filtration for UAE homes
h1: Whole House Water Filtration for UAE Homes
primaryQuestion: Do I need a whole house water filter in the UAE, and how should it be configured?
metaTitle: Whole House Water Filter for the UAE
metaDescription: Point-of-entry filtration for UAE villas: which stages your water justifies, why more stages are not better, and the details that decide serviceability.
directAnswer: A whole-house — point-of-entry — system treats water where it enters the property, so every tap, shower and appliance gets treated water. It is the right answer for complaints about water you do not drink: sediment, chlorine smell in the shower, rust marks, appliance wear. In the UAE it earns its place on villas, because most are tank-fed or tanker-fed and sediment loading is high. It is usually not right for an apartment, and it is not a drinking-water system — it does not remove dissolved solids and it does not disinfect.
keyFacts: Treats every outlet; point-of-use systems treat one
Configured as single, double or triple stage after a water test — more stages are not automatically better
Does not remove dissolved solids and does not disinfect; those are separate stages
Bypass valves, a drain port and clearance to open the housings decide whether it stays maintained

sections.heading: What it is and what it is not
paragraphs: Point-of-entry filtration is a set of large-capacity housings, usually on a steel frame, cut into the incoming supply before it branches to the property. Water passes through them on the way to everything.

What it is not is a drinking-water system. It does not remove dissolved solids, so it will not change a salty or flat taste. It is not a disinfection stage, so it does not address the microbiological risk that storage introduces. And it is not a softener, so it does not stop limescale forming. Understanding those three exclusions is what prevents the most common disappointment: a substantial system fitted, and the original complaint untouched.

sections.heading: Deciding whether your property needs one

list.title: Yes, if you control the incoming line
list.body: Villas and townhouses. This is the basic condition — no point-of-entry treatment is possible without it.

list.title: Yes, if you are tank-fed or tanker-fed
list.body: Which describes most UAE villas and nearly all properties in the northern Emirates and outlying areas. Sediment is the dominant local water complaint and this is where it is intercepted.

list.title: Yes, if your complaint is about water you do not drink
list.body: Shower chlorine, washing-machine sediment, rust staining, appliance wear. None of these have a point-of-use answer.

list.title: Usually no, in an apartment
list.body: You do not control the supply, there is no plant room, and building management must approve work on the riser. Treat the drinking outlet instead.

sections.heading: How the stages are actually chosen
paragraphs: The configuration should follow the water test. This is the part of the specification where money is most often wasted.

list.title: Sediment — almost always
list.body: The first and most valuable stage on nearly every UAE property. On a tanker-fed villa, a self-cleaning version with a reusable mesh you rinse through a valve saves the ongoing cost and nuisance of cartridges that block in weeks.

list.title: Carbon — where chlorine, taste or odour is the complaint
list.body: Removes chlorine at the point of entry, so every shower benefits. Also protects a softener's resin downstream, which is a good reason to fit it even when taste is not the primary complaint.

list.title: Multimedia — where the water justifies it
list.body: Handles a mix of sediment, iron and organics. This is the stage most often sold unnecessarily, and it should be traceable to something in the test result.

list.title: Softener — if hardness is the complaint
list.body: Strictly a separate device rather than a filtration stage, but it belongs in the same specification conversation because it is fitted at the same point and hardness is the most common UAE villa complaint.

list.title: Disinfection — if the property stores water
list.body: UV or a contact-disinfection stage, fitted after filtration. This is the gap we most often find in existing villa installations.

sections.heading: Why triple-stage is not automatically better
paragraphs: Every stage you add costs money twice: once at installation, and again at every service visit for the rest of the system's life. A stage that is not addressing something in your water test is a recurring cost with no return.

There is also a hydraulic cost. Each housing adds pressure drop, and a villa with marginal incoming pressure can end up with visibly weaker flow at the furthest bathroom. Sizing generously and staging minimally is usually a better system than the reverse.

sections.heading: The installation details that decide everything

list.title: Bypass valves
list.body: So the property keeps water during a service. On a villa this is close to essential, and retrofitting it later costs more than fitting it at the start.

list.title: A drain port
list.body: So servicing does not mean draining the villa, and so a self-cleaning stage can actually be flushed.

list.title: Clearance to open the housings
list.body: A system mounted tight against a wall or ceiling is a system that gets serviced badly. The housings have to come off.

list.title: Housing size over stage count
list.body: Large housings give longer cartridge life and better flow. Undersizing to save space is the decision most often regretted.

list.title: Sheltered siting, and stainless fixings near the coast
list.body: Salt-laden air in the coastal communities shortens the life of exposed metalwork noticeably. This is a specification decision, not a finish.

list.title: Trace the lines before cutting in
list.body: Properties with a separate irrigation supply need the filter on the right line. Fitting it on the landscaping line is a real and recurring mistake.

sections.heading: Living with it
paragraphs: Fit a pressure gauge before and after. A growing differential reports a developing blockage before anyone notices the flow dropping, and it turns cartridge intervals from guesswork into a reading.

Set the interval from what the removed cartridges actually look like on this property, not from a manufacturer schedule written for continuous mains supply. And remember that self-cleaning and multimedia stages need their rinse performed properly — skipped rinses are the most common reason a well-specified whole-house system underperforms.

author: aquapure-technical-team

title: What drives the cost of RO installation in Dubai?
h1: What Drives the Cost of RO Installation in Dubai?
primaryQuestion: How much does RO installation cost in Dubai, and what affects the price?
metaDescription: We do not publish a price, and here is why. The six factors that move an RO installation quotation, and how to compare two quotes fairly.
directAnswer: We do not publish a figure, because it would be wrong for most people who read it — and a published 'starting from' price is usually the cheapest possible configuration in the easiest possible kitchen. What moves the number is real: the system your water test justifies, whether a booster pump is needed for your building's pressure, whether a drinking faucet can use an existing tap hole, how far the unit sits from the drain and feed point, whether it is domestic or commercial duty, and whether ongoing servicing is included. A technician quotes on site, in writing, in AED, with no call-out fee.
keyFacts: The specification follows a measured water test, and the specification is most of the cost
A booster pump is a common and legitimate addition on upper floors — not an upsell
Commercial duty changes the sizing entirely; domestic pricing does not transfer
Compare quotes on the whole cost of ownership, including consumables, not on the install price alone

sections.heading: Why we will not print a number
paragraphs: A price on a web page has to describe some specific configuration in some specific property. The moment you publish it, it becomes the number people expect — and the honest range for 'RO installation in Dubai' spans a simple carbon-and-sediment unit in an easy kitchen through to a modular system with a pump and a UV stage in a villa utility room.

The industry's usual answer is a 'starting from' figure, which is technically true and practically misleading: it is almost always the cheapest system in the easiest installation, and very few people end up buying it. We would rather explain what moves the number and then quote your property.

sections.heading: The six things that actually move the quotation

list.title: 1. What your water justifies
list.body: The largest factor, and the one determined by measurement rather than by preference. A high TDS reading points to RO with more stages and possibly remineralisation. A low reading with a chlorine complaint points to a carbon-and-sediment unit that costs considerably less. This is why the test comes first.

list.title: 2. Whether a booster pump is needed
list.body: Determined by static pressure at your tap, which is a function of your floor and your building. On upper floors it is common. It is a genuine part of the system — a starved membrane produces slowly, wastes more and fails early — but it is also a line item, and you should be told why it is there.

list.title: 3. Tanked or tankless
list.body: Tankless costs more for the same filtration. You are buying cupboard space and on-demand production, not better water. If a tanked system fits, it is the cheaper correct answer.

list.title: 4. The installation itself
list.body: Whether a faucet can use an existing tap hole or needs one drilled in stone. How far the unit sits from the drain and the cold feed. Whether isolation valves exist or have to be added. None of these are large individually; together they are the difference between a straightforward fit and a half-day job.

list.title: 5. Domestic or commercial duty
list.body: A cafeteria or an accommodation block is sized on measured throughput, and domestic sizing fails in weeks. Commercial systems are a different category of quotation and are not comparable to a household figure.

list.title: 6. What happens afterwards
list.body: Consumables and servicing are the majority of the lifetime cost. A quote that is cheap on installation and expensive on cartridges is not the cheaper quote — it just presents better.

sections.heading: How to compare two quotations fairly

list.title: Ask for the reading each quote was based on
list.body: If a quotation was produced without measuring your water, it was produced without the main input. Ask what the TDS and hardness readings were and where they were taken.

list.title: Compare stage for stage, not price for price
list.body: A cheaper system with fewer stages may be exactly right for your water — or may be missing the stage that addresses your actual complaint. The specification is the comparison; the price is the consequence.

list.title: Get the consumable cost and interval in writing
list.body: Cartridge formats, how many stages, how often, and what each costs. This is where the lifetime difference lives, and it is the question least often asked.

list.title: Check whether the pump is included or extra
list.body: A quote without a pump on a high floor is not cheaper; it is incomplete.

list.title: Ask what the cartridges are
list.body: Standard formats get serviced on schedule. Proprietary ones tie you to one supplier and wait for deliveries. That is a cost even when it is not a price.

list.title: Be sceptical of pressure
list.body: A limited-time discount on a water filter is a sales technique, not a market condition. A free water test with no obligation should be exactly that.

sections.heading: What you should be able to expect from a quotation

list.title: A measured basis
list.body: Readings taken at your tap, shown to you, with an explanation of what they mean and what they do not.

list.title: A fixed figure in AED, in writing, before work starts
list.body: Not a verbal estimate, and not a figure that moves once the technician is in the cupboard.

list.title: No call-out fee for the visit
list.body: Including in the case where the recommendation is that you need nothing, or that your existing system only needs a cartridge.

list.title: The ongoing cost stated up front
list.body: What the consumables are, how often, and what a service visit involves.

sections.heading: The cheapest correct answer is sometimes nothing
paragraphs: It is worth saying plainly, because it is the outcome no price list can accommodate. If your measured TDS is low, your water tastes fine, and your existing system just needs a cartridge, then a cartridge is the whole recommendation.
That happens often enough that it is a reason to have the water measured before you shop — and a reason to be careful with anyone who arrives with a system already chosen.
